title: Learning the Body
logline: Young novices learn to recite the body's thirty-two parts aloud, forwards and then backwards, stumbling over the reverse order until a teacher corrects them.
human_question: What happens to a body once you have said all thirty-two of its ordinary parts out loud, in order, for weeks?

situation.what_happens: New novices are given the list of the body's thirty-two parts as one of their first lessons. They learn it in small groups of parts, reciting aloud, day after day, first forwards and then backwards, and the reverse order is where it reliably breaks down. A teacher corrects a skipped or misplaced part and the group begins again. Around the lesson runs everything else in the day: sweeping, meals, washing, study, sleep.
situation.who_is_involved: Novices at the very start of their training, some of them children; the teacher who sets and corrects the recitation; the senior monks of the house; the families who placed them there and visit.
situation.what_is_at_stake: For the novices, whether the words will ever become anything more than words, since the texts themselves say the practice only begins when each name calls up the thing. For the teacher, handing on a discipline that can only be handed on by repetition. For the children, a childhood spent learning something whose point is not yet available to them.
situation.how_it_unfolds: A recitation lesson runs for weeks or months before anything is expected of it. It begins as sound, is corrected constantly, and either settles into memory or does not. The sources are clear that whatever change they describe comes slowly, to some people and not others, and nothing about filming can produce it or show it happening.

concept_merge.why_together: C093 contributes the practice itself: thirty-two named parts recited aloud and then mentally, in fixed groups, forwards and backwards, given as the first meditation subject to the newly ordained, with the names treated as a marker to be dropped once the path is worn. C063 contributes the same discipline applied to the world: the sources tell the student to learn the twenty-eight kinds of matter by heart, and treat counting a whole into its parts as a way of attending rather than as information.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Together they show that the two lists in this group, the body's parts and matter's kinds, are one exercise done twice. What is being taught is not an inventory but a way of looking that refuses to accept a single name for a whole. Watching children do it by rote also shows the honest distance between the exercise and its result: the words come first, by years.

concept_links.why: The digest describes the practice exactly: thirty-two parts recited aloud and then mentally, in fixed groups, forwards and backwards, named as the first meditation subject given to the newly ordained, with the names compared to a marker tied on the way to a well and dropped once the path is worn. The digest also states that the aim is to let go of both craving for the body and aversion to it, so the lesson may not be read on screen as self-hatred or as body-praise.

The digest reports the instruction to learn the twenty-eight kinds of matter by heart and treats naming parts one by one as a practice of attention, less a piece of information than a discipline for slowing down the eye. The recitation lesson is that discipline in its most literal form.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: Saying the body's ordinary parts aloud, one by one, forwards and backwards, slowly turns 'my body' from one smooth whole into a list of things. These texts give this as a first lesson to the newly ordained.
what_must_be_real: The novices' actual training, with consent from guardians, the monastery and the novices themselves, renewable at any point. Nothing performed for the camera, and no implication that the children have grasped what they are reciting. Nothing from the sources' longer part-by-part description of the body, its bone, muscle and sinew counts, its intestine lengths, what it says bile does, may appear as anatomy or medicine: the digest records all of it as traditional commentary and rules out its use as fact.
position_hint: middle: it follows the films that take a body apart from outside and turns the same operation inward, before the group moves to how a body begins and how it ends.
risks: Filming minors: consent from guardians and monastery at every stage, and the novices' own willingness.
Cute-child framing that trivialises the practice.
Implying the children understand or have completed what they are still learning by rote.
Traditional anatomy in the sources mistaken for medical description.
Reading the practice as body-shaming or as body-positivity, both of which the digest rules out.
drop_if: No monastery, guardians or novices consent.
No genuine ongoing recitation practice to observe.

connections.note: A body assembled out of sight in one film; the same body, years later, taught to take itself apart again, part by part, in the next.

selection.reason: Used by EPD-0063; the only film carrying C093, and a direct observation of the practice as the sources describe it being taught.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
